title: The Analects: Family, Ritual and the Good Ruler
bigQuestion: How did a teacher who called himself a transmitter, not a maker, come to shape family life, schooling and government across East Asia for more than two thousand years?

story.title: Four Answers to One Question
story.kicker: In a small state in ancient China, a teacher gives four students four different answers to the same question about their parents.
paragraphs: Around 500 BCE, in the state of Lu in eastern China, a teacher in his fifties sits on a mat with a few students. One of them, Meng Yi, a young nobleman, asks what a good son owes his parents. The teacher answers with two words: no disobedience. Later, riding in a carriage, he explains to another student what he meant. While parents live, serve them according to ritual. When they die, bury them according to ritual. Afterward, offer sacrifices to them according to ritual.

Another student, Meng Wu Bo, asks the same question and hears something different: give your parents no cause for anxiety except your health. A third student, Ziyou, asks and is told that people today think feeding their parents is enough. But we also feed dogs and horses, the teacher says. Without reverence, what is the difference? A fourth, Zixia, asks and hears that the hard part is the expression on your face. Doing chores and serving food first is not yet the whole of it.

Why four answers? The students who later wrote these conversations down noticed something about their teacher. He did not hand out a rule. He looked at the person in front of him and said the thing that person most needed to hear. The proud young noble needed to hear about limits. The son who only brought food needed to hear about reverence. The record of these exchanges became the book we call the Analects, compiled by his followers in the generations after his death in 479 BCE.

The teacher was Kong Qiu, known to the world as Confucius. He insisted that he invented nothing and only passed on the ways of the ancient kings. Yet the way he asked about the inside of an action, about reverence and the look on a face, turned old ceremonies into a study of the heart. Within a few centuries, Han officials were trained in the classics he taught, and later every candidate in the imperial examinations would memorize his words. Today students in Qufu, Seoul, Hanoi and Chicago's Chinatown still read them, and this chapter reads them too.
story.think: Confucius gave four students four different answers to one question. What does that suggest about how he thought teaching should work, and how should it change the way we read a book made of such answers?

lessons.title: The Zhou and the Mandate of Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius looked back to the early Zhou kings, whose right to rule rested on the idea that Heaven gives its mandate to the virtuous and takes it from the cruel.
reading: In museums in Beijing, Taipei and Chicago you can see bronze vessels cast about three thousand years ago. Inside some of them is a text: a record of a gift from a Zhou king to a noble, cast into the metal so the noble's descendants would remember it. The *Zhou dynasty* (c. 1046–256 BCE) came to power by overthrowing the Shang. To explain why that was right, Zhou texts said that *tian*, Heaven, had withdrawn its favor from the last Shang king because of his cruelty and given it to the Zhou.

This idea is called the *Mandate of Heaven*. In these texts Heaven is not a person with a face and a name like the God of the Hebrew Bible. It is the high moral power that orders the world. The king is the Son of Heaven, but only on condition: he must rule with virtue. Floods, famines and rebellions could be read as signs that the mandate was slipping away. A dynasty that lost its virtue could rightly be replaced. That is different from a claim that a king rules by a divine right that can never be lost.

The early Zhou produced the heroes Confucius admired most: King Wen, King Wu, who defeated the Shang, and the Duke of Zhou, who governed loyally for his young nephew and then handed power back. Confucius held the Duke of Zhou up as the model of the good minister. In the Analects he sighs that he has grown old because he no longer dreams of the Duke. Two collections that preserve Zhou material, the Book of Documents and the Book of Songs, are quoted by Confucius constantly.

Notice what counted as sacred in this world. Kings sacrificed to Heaven and to their royal ancestors. Noble families kept ancestral temples and followed detailed ceremonies. The specialists who preserved and taught these ceremonies were called *ru*, a word that later meant scholars. Confucius belonged to this class, and his followers were called ru. What English calls Confucianism is, in Chinese, rujia, the school of the ru. The tradition was never named after him at home.

words.d: the Chinese dynasty (c. 1046–256 BCE) whose early kings Confucius took as models of good rule
Heaven; in early Chinese thought, the high moral power that orders the world and judges rulers
the idea that Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and withdraws it from a cruel one
the ritual specialists and scholars of ancient China; the Chinese name for Confucianism is rujia, the school of the ru

look.title: Two Ways to Hold a Throne
look.text: Idea A: A king rules because Heaven has granted him the mandate. Heaven judges by his virtue. If he becomes cruel, floods and revolts show that the mandate is passing to someone else. Idea B: A king rules because God appointed his family, and no failure of his can cancel that appointment. Subjects owe him obedience no matter how he rules.
look.prompt: Under each idea, what may a people do about a cruel king, and what would each idea say a rebellion proves? Which idea gives a ruler more reason to govern well?

check.q: What did the Mandate of Heaven mean in Zhou texts?
choices: Heaven's approval of a ruler, which depends on his virtue and can be withdrawn
A written contract between the king and his nobles
The king's promise to sacrifice to Heaven once a year
A guarantee that the royal family would rule forever
check.why: The mandate was conditional: Heaven gave it to the virtuous Zhou and took it from the cruel last Shang king, so it could be lost.

check.q: Which collection of Zhou-era material did Confucius quote constantly?
choices: The Daodejing
The Book of Songs
The Analects
The Classic of Filial Piety
check.why: The Book of Songs and the Book of Documents preserve early Zhou material, and Confucius drew on both; the other three came after him.

check.q: Who were the ru?
choices: The kings of the Shang dynasty
Soldiers in the Zhou army
Ritual specialists and scholars, the class Confucius's followers were named for
Buddhist monks in early China
check.why: Ru were the specialists who kept the old ceremonies; Confucianism in Chinese is rujia, the school of the ru.

lessons.title: A World Coming Apart
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius taught in the Spring and Autumn period, when Zhou authority had collapsed and rival thinkers competed to explain how order could be restored.
reading: In 771 BCE, invaders sacked the Zhou capital and the court fled east to Luoyang. The king kept his title, but real power passed to the lords of the regional states. Historians call the next centuries the *Spring and Autumn period* (771–476 BCE), after a chronicle kept in the state of Lu, Confucius's home. It was followed by the *Warring States* period (475–221 BCE). Many smaller states were swallowed until seven large ones remained, fighting with iron weapons and armies of conscripted farmers.

The old order of hereditary nobles was crumbling. Ministers pushed aside their lords; lords ignored the king. The great question of the age was how to bring back order. Traditional accounts speak of a Hundred Schools of thought. The Confucians answered with ritual and moral example. The Mohists, followers of Mozi, taught impartial care for everyone and opposed costly wars and funerals. The Legalists answered with strict laws, harsh punishments and a powerful state. Daoists, whom the next chapter studies, answered by returning to the Way. These were not only philosophies; they were also advice offered by traveling teachers to rulers looking for help.

The Legalist answer won first. The western state of Qin, reorganized by the Legalist minister Shang Yang, conquered its rivals and unified China in 221 BCE under the First Emperor. Later Confucian historians told with horror how his government burned privately held books and executed scholars. The Qin dynasty fell within fifteen years of its founding. The Han dynasty that replaced it eventually turned to the ru and their classics, and the rest of this chapter follows that turn.

For a reader, the background matters. The Analects was assembled during this age of argument. When Confucius says that people led by laws and punishments will simply dodge punishment, while people led by virtue and ritual will develop a sense of shame, he is taking one side of a live debate. Nearly every saying in the book is an answer to someone. Reading it well means asking who he is answering.

words.d: the era (771–476 BCE) of weak Zhou kings and rival states, named for a chronicle of the state of Lu
the period (475–221 BCE) when seven large states fought until Qin unified China
a traditional name for the many competing schools of thought in China before 221 BCE
the school that taught order through strict law, harsh punishment and a strong state; adopted by Qin

look.title: Law or Virtue
look.text: The Master said, 'If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame. If they be led by virtue, and uniformity sought to be given them by the rules of propriety, they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good.'
look.prompt: Which approach to government, later championed by the Legalists, does Confucius reject here, and what does he claim laws alone cannot produce in people?

check.q: The Spring and Autumn period takes its name from what?
choices: The two seasons when armies could march
A poem by Confucius
The Zhou royal calendar
A chronicle kept in the state of Lu
check.why: The period is named for the Spring and Autumn Annals, a chronicle of Lu, Confucius's home state.

check.q: Which school answered the disorder of the age with strict laws and harsh punishments?
choices: Legalism
Mohism
Confucianism
Daoism
check.why: Legalists such as Shang Yang built the Qin state on law and punishment; Mohists taught impartial care, Confucians ritual and virtue.

check.q: In Analects 2.3, what does Confucius say is missing in people who are governed only by punishments?
choices: Wealth
A sense of shame
Fear of the ruler
Knowledge of the law
check.why: He says such people avoid punishment but have no sense of shame; only virtue and ritual produce that inner sense.

lessons.title: Kong Qiu of Lu
lessons.mainIdea: Confucius (551–479 BCE) was a teacher from the state of Lu whose ideas outlived his failure to find a ruler who would put them into practice.
reading: His name was Kong Qiu. His students called him Kongzi or Kong Fuzi, Master Kong, and Jesuit missionaries in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries turned that into the Latin name *Confucius*. He was born in 551 BCE near *Qufu*, in the state of Lu, in what is now Shandong province. His family belonged to the lowest rank of the nobility, and his father died when he was small. Later sources say he worked as a young man keeping accounts for granaries and tending herds. He mastered the six arts of a gentleman: ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing and arithmetic.

Tradition says he held office in Lu, perhaps as minister of crime, though the details are uncertain. Around 497 BCE he left, disappointed with the ruler, and spent roughly fourteen years traveling from state to state with a band of disciples, offering his services. In Wei, Song, Chen and Cai he found polite interest and no real job, and at least once his party nearly starved. He returned to Lu about 484 BCE, taught, and by tradition edited the old classics. He died in 479 BCE and was buried at Qufu, where the Kong family cemetery and a great temple in his honor still stand.

His teaching had a new feature. He took students without regard to birth, saying that in teaching there should be no distinction between classes, and that he had never refused anyone who came with even a small gift for the lesson. His disciples included Yan Hui, the poor and brilliant favorite who died young; Zilu, brave and blunt; Zigong, a merchant and diplomat; and Zengzi, who carried the school forward. Tradition counts seventy-two close disciples out of some three thousand students.

How did he see himself? In the Analects he calls himself a transmitter and not a maker, one who believes in and loves the ancients. Yet his focus on the inner motive behind ritual was new. He said little about spirits and the afterlife. Later Confucians honored him as the Supreme Sage and First Teacher, and some treated him as nearly divine, while others in the tradition rejected that. Historians read him as a moral teacher and would-be reformer whose real success came only after his death.

words.d: the Latin form of Kong Fuzi, Master Kong (551–479 BCE), the teacher whose sayings fill the Analects
the town in Shandong province where Confucius was born and buried; site of his temple and family cemetery
a committed student who follows a teacher; Confucius's disciples preserved his sayings
the skills of an ancient Chinese gentleman: ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing and arithmetic

look.title: Dates to Keep in Order
look.cite: traditional dates from Sima Qian's Records (c. 100 BCE) and modern scholarship
look.prompt: About how many years did Confucius spend traveling, and how long after his death did Qin unify China? Why does a BCE date get smaller as time goes forward?

check.q: Where does the name Confucius come from?
choices: It is the name his parents gave him
It is the Chinese word for teacher
It is a Latin form of Kong Fuzi made by Jesuit missionaries
It was a title given by the Han emperor
check.why: His name was Kong Qiu; students called him Kong Fuzi, and Jesuits centuries later latinized that as Confucius.

check.q: How did Confucius describe his own role in the Analects?
choices: As a prophet sent by Heaven
As the founder of a new religion
As a king in waiting
As a transmitter and not a maker
check.why: He claimed only to pass on the ways of the ancients, though his stress on inner motive was in fact new.

check.q: What was new about the way Confucius taught?
choices: He accepted students regardless of their birth
He taught only the sons of rulers
He refused to teach ritual or music
He wrote a textbook for every student
check.why: He said there should be no distinction of classes in teaching and took poor students like Yan Hui as well as nobles.

lessons.title: A Book of Sayings
lessons.mainIdea: The Analects is a collection of short sayings and dialogues compiled by Confucius's followers over generations, so it must be read as a record of conversations, not a treatise.
reading: Open the *Analects* and you find twenty short books holding about five hundred passages. Most begin the same way: The Master said. The Chinese title, Lunyu, means something like selected sayings. Confucius did not write the book. His disciples and their own students compiled it over the fifth to third centuries BCE, and scholars can see earlier and later layers in it. A passage may be a single *aphorism*, a short pointed saying, or a brief dialogue with a named student or ruler.

This form demands a certain kind of reading. A treatise explains itself; a record of conversations does not. The reader must ask who is speaking, who is asking and why. In one passage two students ask the identical question, whether they should act at once on what they learn. Bold Zilu is told to consult his father and elder brother first. Cautious Ran You is told to act at once. A third student asks why, and Confucius answers that one needed holding back and the other needed pushing forward.

The English version this course quotes is by *James Legge*, a Scottish missionary and scholar in Hong Kong who published the Analects in 1861 as the first volume of his Chinese Classics. His translation is in the public domain and still widely read. It uses older spellings, so Zigong appears as Tsze-kung, and it renders key terms in Victorian English: propriety for li, benevolence or perfect virtue for ren, the superior man for junzi. When you meet those phrases, translate them back.

From the twelfth century on, the Analects was read as one of the *Four Books*, together with the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. Apply the toolkit from the start of this course. Author: many hands over generations. Audience: students preparing to serve in government. Purpose: to preserve a teacher's way of living and to train character. Genre: teaching, in the form of sayings. Like the Gospels or the hadith, it is a record of a teacher kept by followers, but it contains no miracles and almost nothing about the divine.

words.d: Lunyu, the collection of Confucius's sayings and dialogues compiled by his followers after his death
a short, pointed saying that states a truth or a principle
Scottish missionary-scholar (1815–1897) whose public-domain English translations of the Chinese classics this course quotes
the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean, the core Confucian curriculum from the twelfth century on

look.title: The Opening Lines
look.text: The Master said, 'Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?'
look.prompt: The book opens with three questions about learning, friendship and being ignored. What kind of person do these three lines describe, and why might the compilers have chosen them to come first?

check.q: Who wrote the Analects?
choices: Confucius, late in his life
Confucius's disciples and their students, over generations
James Legge
The First Emperor of Qin
check.why: The Lunyu was compiled by followers across the fifth to third centuries BCE; Legge only translated it in 1861.

check.q: Why did Confucius tell Zilu to wait and Ran You to act at once?
choices: Zilu had broken a ritual rule
Ran You was older
He fitted his answer to each student's character
He had changed his mind between the questions
check.why: He explained that the bold student needed holding back and the cautious one needed pushing forward.

check.q: In Legge's translation, the word propriety stands for which Chinese term?
choices: ren
junzi
xiao
li
check.why: Legge rendered li as propriety or the rules of propriety; ren became benevolence and junzi the superior man.

lessons.title: Ren: The Humane Heart
lessons.mainIdea: Ren, translated humaneness or benevolence, is the highest virtue in the Analects: care for other people as the root from which all other goodness grows.
reading: The Chinese character for *ren* is written with the sign for person beside the sign for two. Humaneness is what shows itself between two people. When the disciple Fan Chi asks what ren is, Confucius answers that it is to love others. When Yan Hui asks, he is told that ren means mastering oneself and returning to ritual. When Zhong Gong asks, he hears that he should not do to others what he would not want done to himself. As with filial piety, the answer bends toward the questioner.

That last answer is the famous rule of *shu*, usually translated reciprocity or consideration. Asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius offers shu and states it in the negative: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. The Jewish teacher Hillel, some five centuries later, put a similar rule in nearly the same negative form, and the Gospel of Matthew records Jesus stating it positively. Scholars still debate whether the negative form asks less than the positive one or simply protects others from our assumptions about what they want. The disciple Zengzi summarized the Master's way in two words: *zhong*, doing one's utmost, and shu.

Ren is demanding. Confucius rarely called anyone ren, and he declined the title for himself. Ren is not softness, either: he says only the person of ren knows how to love and how to dislike, because that person's feelings are rightly ordered. Above all, ren gives ritual its meaning. If a person lacks ren, he asks, what has that person to do with rites or with music? The outward ceremony without the inward heart is an empty shell.

Later Confucians built on this. Mencius said ren is simply the human heart. Neo-Confucians of the Song dynasty said the person of ren feels one body with all things. Translators have offered goodness, humaneness, benevolence and authoritative conduct, and none is perfect. The idea to hold is that in Confucian thought the inner root of goodness is a felt care for others, and every visible virtue grows from it.

words.d: humaneness or benevolence; the highest Confucian virtue, care for others as the root of all goodness
reciprocity or consideration: not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself
doing one's utmost; loyalty or wholehearted effort, paired with shu in Zengzi's summary of the Master's way
treating others as you would want to be treated; the principle behind the rule in Analects 15.23

look.title: One Word for a Lifetime
look.text: Tsze-kung asked, saying, 'Is there one word which may serve as a rule of practice for all one's life?' The Master said, 'Is not Reciprocity such a word? What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.'
look.prompt: Restate this rule in the positive form found in Matthew 7:12. Think of one situation where the two forms would lead to different actions.

check.q: The character for ren combines the signs for which two things?
choices: Person and two
Heart and king
Heaven and earth
Father and son
check.why: Ren is written as person plus two: humaneness as it appears between people.

check.q: According to Zengzi, the Master's whole way came down to what?
choices: Ritual and music
Zhong and shu: doing one's utmost and consideration for others
Obedience to the king and to Heaven
Study and examination
check.why: Zengzi summarized the way of Confucius as zhong (wholehearted effort) and shu (reciprocity).

check.q: How is the rule of Confucius like the rule attributed to Hillel?
choices: Both say to love enemies
Both are found in the Book of Songs
Both state the rule negatively: do not do what you would not want done to you
Both apply only to family members
check.why: Confucius and Hillel both phrase the rule in the negative, while the Gospel of Matthew records a positive form.

lessons.title: Li: Ritual and Propriety
lessons.mainIdea: Li, meaning ritual, ceremony and the courtesies of daily life, is how ren takes visible form in the Confucian view, and how a society holds together without force.
reading: Book Ten of the Analects reads almost like a stage direction. It describes how Confucius behaved at court: how he bowed, how he lifted the hem of his robe on the steps, how he would not sit on a mat that was crooked, how he did not talk while eating. All of this is *li*. The word covers the great sacrifices to ancestors, the three years of mourning for a parent, the ceremonies of a royal court, and small things like how to greet an elder. Translators use rites, ritual, *propriety* and etiquette, and all of them are part of it.

Li is not empty form. When Lin Fang asks about the root of ritual, Confucius answers that in ceremonies it is better to be simple than lavish, and in mourning it is better to feel real grief than to attend to every detail. But the form still matters. When Zigong wanted to drop the sheep offered at the monthly announcement of the new moon, Confucius told him: you love the sheep; I love the ceremony. In the Confucian view, practicing the form trains the feeling. Li is where a person actually does ren.

Li also governs. Confucius says that a leader who governs by virtue is like the north star, which stays in place while the other stars turn around it. The character of a ruler is like wind, he tells a powerful minister, and the people are like grass that bends under it. Asked how he would begin to govern, he says he would start with the *rectification of names*: making words match reality. A ruler must act like a ruler, a minister like a minister, a father like a father, a son like a son. When titles and conduct come apart, order fails.

It helps to compare. In its reach into daily life, li resembles halakhah, the Jewish way of law, and Hindu dharma. But li is not commanded by a god in a revealed scripture. Its authority comes from the ancient sages who shaped it and from its proven effect on human character. Confucians today debate how much of the old li still applies. Few observe three years of mourning, yet the idea that form shapes feeling remains central to the tradition.

words.d: ritual, ceremony and proper conduct, from great sacrifices to everyday courtesy; the outward form of ren
Legge's word for li: correct, fitting behavior in a given role and situation
Confucius's principle that titles and conduct must match: a ruler must act as a ruler, a father as a father
the ceremonies and periods of grief after a death; Confucian tradition prescribed three years for a parent

look.title: When the Prince Is Prince
look.text: The Duke Ching, of Ch'î, asked Confucius about government. Confucius replied, 'There is government, when the prince is prince, and the minister is minister; when the father is father, and the son is son.'
look.prompt: What does it mean for a father to be a father in this saying? Give an example from daily life where a title and a person's conduct have come apart, and say what Confucius would ask to be fixed first.

check.q: Which of these is an example of li?
choices: Feeling compassion for a stranger
Passing the civil-service examination
Knowing the meaning of the Dao
The way a person bows, dresses and speaks at a ceremony
check.why: Li is ritual and proper conduct, from great ceremonies to everyday courtesy; compassion itself belongs to ren.

check.q: What did Confucius tell Lin Fang about the root of ritual?
choices: Real grief in mourning matters more than lavish detail
Ritual should be as expensive as possible
Only rulers need to perform rituals
Ritual has no root; it is pure custom
check.why: He said simplicity beats lavishness and genuine grief beats attention to every detail.

check.q: What does the rectification of names call for?
choices: Giving every child a new name at adulthood
Making titles and conduct match: a father should act like a father
Renaming states after their rulers
Writing all names in the ancient script
check.why: Confucius said good government requires that the prince be a prince, the minister a minister, the father a father.

lessons.title: Xiao and the Five Relationships
lessons.mainIdea: Filial piety, xiao, is the first school of virtue in Confucian thought, and it opens into five relationships that order all of society.
reading: Return to the story that opened this chapter. Four students asked about *xiao*, filial piety, the respect, care and deference a child owes to parents and, beyond them, to ancestors. In the Analects the disciple Youzi calls filial piety and respect for elder brothers the root of ren. An early text compiled by Han times, the *Classic of Filial Piety*, opens by saying that our bodies come from our parents and that not harming them is where filial piety begins. In this view, you first learn to care for others at home.

Xiao is not blind obedience. Confucius says that a son who sees his parents doing wrong should *remonstrate* gently, and if they will not listen, should remain respectful and not complain. Later Confucian writers went further and said a son who never remonstrates is not filial at all. The tradition also faced hard cases. A governor boasts of a man who reported his own father for stealing a sheep. Confucius answers that in his region uprightness looks different: a father shields his son and a son shields his father. Legalists rejected that answer, and ethicists still argue about it.

From the family, Confucian thought moves outward through the *five relationships*: ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder brother and younger brother, friend and friend. The book of Mencius attaches a virtue to each: duty, affection, distinction, order and trust. Four are between unequals and one is between equals. Each side has obligations: the ruler must be humane, not only the minister loyal. Historically the tradition placed women under the authority of fathers, husbands and sons, and the Han scholar Ban Zhao wrote a widely read guide to a woman's proper conduct. Modern Confucians and their critics debate how much of that belongs to the core of the teaching.

The concept here is sometimes called role ethics. A person becomes good by filling roles well, beginning with the closest ones. The Great Learning lays out the chain: cultivate yourself, regulate your family, order the state, and bring peace to all under Heaven. Compare the commandment in Exodus 20:12 to honor father and mother. Both traditions place honor for parents near the center, but the Confucian version makes the family the training ground for every other virtue.

words.d: filial piety: the respect, care and deference owed to parents and ancestors
Xiaojing, a short early Confucian text, compiled by Han times, on the duties of children to parents and subjects to rulers
to object respectfully; Confucius said a child should gently remonstrate with parents who do wrong
ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, friend and friend

look.title: The Stolen Sheep
look.text: A governor tells Confucius, proudly, that in his district there is an upright man: when his father stole a sheep, the son testified against him. Confucius replies that in his own district uprightness is different. There, fathers shield their sons and sons shield their fathers, and uprightness is found in that. A Legalist official hearing this would say that a state cannot survive if family loyalty outranks the law.
look.prompt: State the strongest case for Confucius's answer and the strongest case for the Legalist's. Where would American law today come down, and does that settle the moral question?

check.q: According to Confucius, what should a son do when he believes his parents are doing wrong?
choices: Obey silently no matter what
Report them to the authorities
Remonstrate gently and stay respectful even if they do not listen
Leave home until they change
check.why: The Analects says to object gently, and if the parents refuse, to remain respectful and not complain.

check.q: Which of the five relationships is between equals?
choices: Ruler and minister
Father and son
Husband and wife
Friend and friend
check.why: Four relationships are between unequals; friendship is the one between equals, with trust as its virtue.

check.q: In what order does the Great Learning say good order spreads?
choices: Self, family, state, all under Heaven
State, family, self, Heaven
Heaven, ruler, minister, people
Friend, brother, parent, ruler
check.why: The Great Learning moves outward: cultivate the self, regulate the family, order the state, bring peace to the world.

lessons.title: Becoming a Junzi
lessons.mainIdea: The junzi, once a word for a nobleman by birth, became in the Analects the person of cultivated character that anyone might become through learning.
reading: The word *junzi* literally means a lord's son, a nobleman by birth. Confucius kept the word and changed its meaning. In the Analects a junzi is a person of moral nobility, contrasted again and again with the *xiaoren*, the small person. The junzi understands what is right, *yi*; the small person understands profit. The junzi is broad-minded and not a partisan; the small person is a partisan and not broad-minded. The junzi looks for the cause of failure in himself; the small person looks for it in others. Legge called the junzi the superior man; modern translators prefer gentleman or exemplary person.

How does one become a junzi? Through learning, xue, which is more than reading. In the most personal passage of the book, Confucius describes his own life as a series of stages: bent on learning at fifteen, standing firm at thirty, free of doubts at forty, knowing the decrees of Heaven at fifty, and able at seventy to follow his heart's desire without overstepping what is right. He warns that learning without thinking is wasted, and thinking without learning is dangerous. Poetry, ritual and music each play a part: the Songs awaken a person, ritual establishes him, and music completes him.

Above the junzi stands the sage, and Confucius denied being one. *Self-cultivation* never ends. Standing by a river, he is recorded as saying that things pass on like this, never ceasing day or night. He also insisted that people enlarge the Way, not the Way people: goodness depends on human effort. That is why the tradition later put such weight on teachers and schools.

The concept behind all this is what philosophers call virtue ethics. Character is formed by practice, the way a musician is formed by playing, rather than by following a list of rules. Buddhists also describe a path of self-transformation, but the goal differs: Confucians aim at harmony among people in this world, not release from the cycle of rebirth. Keep that difference in view when a later unit compares the traditions.

words.d: originally a lord's son; in the Analects, the exemplary person of cultivated character (Legge: the superior man)
the small person, guided by profit and partisanship; the opposite of the junzi
rightness or righteousness: doing what is fitting regardless of gain
the lifelong Confucian practice of forming one's own character through learning, ritual and reflection

look.title: A Life in Six Lines
look.text: The Master said, 'At fifteen, I had my mind bent on learning. At thirty, I stood firm. At forty, I had no doubts. At fifty, I knew the decrees of Heaven. At sixty, my ear was an obedient organ for the reception of truth. At seventy, I could follow what my heart desired, without transgressing what was right.'
look.prompt: What changes between forty and seventy in this account? Why might a tradition that values rules end its founder's story with a heart that no longer needs them?

check.q: What did the word junzi originally mean?
choices: A teacher of ritual
The son of a lord, a noble by birth
A person who has passed the examinations
A Daoist hermit
check.why: Junzi meant a lord's son; Confucius reused it for moral nobility that anyone could attain.

check.q: In Analects 2.4, what does Confucius say happened to him at forty?
choices: He knew the decrees of Heaven
He began to learn
He had no doubts
He stood firm
check.why: The sequence runs: learning at fifteen, standing firm at thirty, no doubts at forty, knowing Heaven's decrees at fifty.

check.q: How does the Analects contrast the junzi with the xiaoren?
choices: The junzi is rich; the small person is poor
The junzi rules; the small person farms
The junzi is old; the small person is young
The junzi is guided by what is right; the small person by profit
check.why: Analects 4.16 says the junzi understands yi, rightness, while the small person understands profit.

lessons.title: Mencius, Xunzi and Human Nature
lessons.mainIdea: After Confucius, Mencius argued that human nature is good and Xunzi that it must be shaped by effort, and the tradition carried both voices forward.
reading: Imagine, says *Mencius*, that you suddenly see a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone at all, he argues, would feel a jolt of alarm and compassion, not to win the parents' thanks or a good reputation, but simply because that is what human hearts do. Mencius (Mengzi, c. 372–289 BCE) lived a century after Confucius and became the tradition's second great voice. From that scene he drew his central claim: human nature is good. The feeling of compassion is the sprout of ren; shame is the sprout of yi; deference is the sprout of li; approving and disapproving is the sprout of wisdom. These *four sprouts* need tending, like seedlings, but they are already there.

Mencius said human nature tends to good as water tends to flow downhill. Bad people are like Ox Mountain, once forested and stripped bare by axes and grazing until visitors assumed it had always been barren. He took the Mandate of Heaven seriously and read it through the people: Heaven sees as the people see. He said that of the three parts of a state, the people matter most and the ruler least, and that a king who abandons humaneness and rightness is no longer a king but a mere fellow whose overthrow is not the killing of a ruler. Like Confucius, he never found a ruler who took the advice.

*Xunzi* (c. 310–c. 235 BCE) disagreed sharply. *Human nature*, he wrote, is bad, or at least crude and self-seeking; goodness is the product of deliberate effort. People become good the way warped wood becomes straight, by being steamed and pressed against a frame. The frame is ritual, teachers and study. Xunzi also treated Heaven as the regular course of nature rather than a moral judge, and said rituals exist for the good they do people, whether or not spirits attend. Two of his students, Han Feizi and Li Si, went on to become leading Legalists, which later Confucians held against him.

For a while Xunzi's realism was the more influential. In the long run Mencius won: the Song dynasty scholar Zhu Xi made the Mencius one of the Four Books, and the tradition called Mencius the Second Sage. Yet Confucians kept reading both. The disagreement shows something worth remembering about every tradition in this course: a living teaching contains arguments, and the arguments are part of what it hands down.

words.d: Mengzi (c. 372–289 BCE), the Confucian thinker who taught that human nature is good; called the Second Sage
Mencius's term for the inborn beginnings of ren, yi, li and wisdom: compassion, shame, deference and moral judgment
Confucian thinker (c. 310–c. 235 BCE) who taught that human nature is crude and goodness comes from effort and ritual
xing, what people are like at birth; the subject of the debate between Mencius and Xunzi

look.title: The Child at the Well
look.text: Mencius: Suppose a person suddenly sees a child about to fall into a well. That person will feel alarm and compassion at once, and not because of any reward or reputation. This shows that the beginning of humaneness is in everyone. Xunzi: A hungry person wants to eat first, and a tired person wants to rest first. If people simply followed their nature, they would fight over goods. Goodness is what teachers and ritual make out of us.
look.prompt: What would Xunzi say about the child at the well, and what would Mencius say about the hungry person? Which explanation better fits what you have seen in people, and what evidence would change your mind?

check.q: What did Mencius conclude from the story of the child at the well?
choices: Everyone has a natural sprout of compassion
People act only for reward
Children should be watched more carefully
Wells should be covered by law
check.why: Mencius argued the instant alarm and compassion show that the beginning of ren is inborn in all people.

check.q: According to Xunzi, where does human goodness come from?
choices: From an inborn good nature
From deliberate effort and training in ritual
From the direct command of Heaven
From wealth and comfort
check.why: Xunzi compared people to warped wood straightened by a frame: goodness is made by teachers, study and ritual.

check.q: Which two students of Xunzi became leading Legalists?
choices: Yan Hui and Zilu
Mencius and Zengzi
Han Feizi and Li Si
Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming
check.why: Han Feizi and Li Si studied under Xunzi and helped shape the Legalist Qin state, which later Confucians held against him.

lessons.title: Scholars, Examinations and the State
lessons.mainIdea: From the Han dynasty until 1905, Confucian texts were the curriculum of government, tested by civil-service examinations that shaped Chinese society.
reading: The Han emperor Wu (reigned 141–87 BCE), advised by the scholar Dong Zhongshu, made the Confucian classics the basis of official learning and founded an Imperial Academy in 124 BCE to teach them. The curriculum was the *Five Classics*: the Book of Songs, the Book of Documents, the Book of Rites, the Book of Changes and the Spring and Autumn Annals. Han Confucianism blended these with theories of yin and yang and the cycles of nature, so that a ruler's conduct was believed to affect harvests and eclipses.

The *civil-service examinations* began under the Sui dynasty in 605 CE and grew under the Tang and Song into the main road to office. Candidates worked through county, provincial and palace levels; the highest degree, jinshi, could take decades and most never earned it. From 1313 the tests were based on the Four Books with the commentaries of *Zhu Xi*. Women could not sit the exams, and wealthy families could afford the years of tutoring, yet in principle almost any man could try, and some poor candidates did rise. Korea adopted similar examinations in 958 and Vietnam in 1075. China abolished them in 1905, after thirteen centuries.

Zhu Xi (1130–1200) also reshaped the philosophy. His *Neo-Confucianism* explained the world through principle, li, written with a different character from the li of ritual, and vital energy, qi. He set the Four Books above the Five Classics and turned self-cultivation into a disciplined program of study and quiet sitting. The Ming thinker Wang Yangming (1472–1529) answered that moral knowledge is innate and that knowing and acting are one. Neo-Confucianism became the ruling teaching of Joseon Korea (1392–1897), influenced Tokugawa Japan and shaped Vietnam.

In the twentieth century the tradition was blamed for China's weakness. Reformers of the May Fourth era around 1919 attacked it, and during the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) Confucius was denounced and temples were damaged. Since the 1980s the Chinese government has revived ceremonies at Qufu and named its overseas language institutes after him. Scholars debate how much of that revival is philosophy and how much is politics. Either way, the sayings of a jobless teacher from Lu remain state business twenty-five centuries later.

words.d: the Songs, Documents, Rites, Changes and Spring and Autumn Annals: the Han-era Confucian canon
the tests on Confucian texts (605–1905 CE) that selected officials for the Chinese state
Song dynasty scholar (1130–1200) whose Neo-Confucian commentaries on the Four Books became the examination standard
the Song and later revival of Confucian thought, explaining the world through principle and vital energy and stressing study

lessons.title: Ancestors and the Qingming Festival
lessons.mainIdea: Ancestor veneration, caring for the dead as continuing members of the family, is the practice where Confucian ethics most clearly looks like religion.
reading: Early in April, families across China, Taiwan and Chinese communities abroad, including in Chicago, drive to cemeteries. They pull weeds from a grave, set out fruit and cooked dishes, light incense, burn paper offerings and bow. This is *Qingming*, the Clear and Bright festival, which falls about fifteen days after the spring equinox. At home many families keep an *ancestral tablet*, a wooden plaque bearing an ancestor's name, on a shelf where offerings are placed on death anniversaries and at the New Year.

*Ancestor veneration* is older than Confucius, and he did not explain it so much as fold it into filial piety. Asked about serving the spirits of the dead, he replied that one who cannot yet serve the living cannot serve spirits, and asked about death, he said that one who does not understand life cannot understand death. He said to respect spirits while keeping them at a distance, and to sacrifice to the ancestors as if they were present. The Doctrine of the Mean sums up the Confucian view: serve the dead as you served them living. Xunzi added that rites give form to human feeling whether or not any spirit attends.

The practice grew institutions. Lineages in southern China built ancestral halls holding rows of tablets. Every county seat had a temple to Confucius himself, where officials offered sacrifices in spring and autumn before tablets of the Master and his disciples. Taiwan marks his traditional birthday, September 28, as Teachers' Day with a dawn ceremony. Since the 1980s the ceremony at Qufu has been revived on a large scale.

Is this worship? The question is old. In the seventeenth century Jesuit missionaries in China argued that the rites to ancestors and to Confucius were civil customs that Catholic converts could keep. Dominican and Franciscan missionaries disagreed and called them idolatry. In 1704 and 1715 the pope forbade converts to take part, the Kangxi emperor restricted Christian missions in response, and the ban was not lifted until 1939. This *Chinese Rites Controversy* shows that whether Confucianism counts as a religion has been argued for centuries, and the answer has had real consequences.

words.d: honoring and making offerings to deceased family members as continuing members of the family
the Clear and Bright festival in early April, when families clean graves and make offerings to ancestors
a wooden plaque bearing an ancestor's name, kept in a home shrine or ancestral hall for offerings
the 17th–18th century dispute over whether Catholic converts could keep rites to ancestors and Confucius

look.title: Serving the Living First
look.text: Chî Lû asked about serving the spirits of the dead. The Master said, 'While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?' Chî Lû added, 'I venture to ask about death?' He was answered, 'While you do not know life, how can you know about death?'
look.prompt: Does Confucius deny that spirits exist, refuse to discuss them, or redirect the question? Support your answer from the words themselves, and say what a Jesuit and a Dominican in the Rites Controversy might each have made of it.

check.q: What is Qingming?
choices: The Confucian name for the Mandate of Heaven
A Han dynasty examination
A spring festival when families clean graves and make offerings to ancestors
The birthday of Confucius
check.why: Qingming, Clear and Bright, falls in early April and is the main day for tending graves and honoring ancestors.

check.q: How did Confucius answer Zilu's question about death?
choices: The soul returns to Heaven
Death is followed by rebirth
Spirits punish the unfilial
While you do not know life, how can you know about death?
check.why: In Analects 11.11 he turns the question back to life, just as he turned the question about spirits back to serving people.

choices: Whether Catholic converts could keep rites to ancestors and Confucius
Whether Buddhists could build temples in China
Whether women could take the examinations
Whether the Analects should be translated
check.why: Jesuits called the rites civil customs; other orders called them idolatry; the pope banned them in the early 1700s.

lessons.title: Philosophy, Ethics or Religion?
lessons.mainIdea: Whether Confucianism is a religion depends on what the word religion is taken to mean, and people in East Asia have answered in more than one way.
reading: At the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, a Chinese diplomat presented a long paper on Confucianism alongside speakers for Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism and Christianity. Its presence raised a question: did a tradition with no creed, no priesthood and no clear god belong at a parliament of religions? Chinese had no exact older equivalent of the Western word religion. The modern term *zongjiao* took on that meaning through Japanese in the late nineteenth century. Before that, Chinese spoke of *jiao*, teachings, and of the *three teachings*: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism.

The case for calling Confucianism a philosophy or an ethic is strong. Its focus is this life and human relationships. It makes few claims about gods, has no church or congregation, and seeks no converts. The case for calling it religious is also strong. It speaks of Heaven and Heaven's mandate. It prescribes sacrifices to ancestors and to Confucius, keeps sacred texts and temples, and offers a path of self-transformation that some modern Confucian scholars describe in religious terms. Some scholars split the difference with the phrase *religious humanism*.

Governments have answered differently. Indonesia lists Confucianism as one of its six officially recognized religions. In mainland China the government classes it as culture and philosophy rather than as one of the five recognized religions. In South Korea, where Confucian family rites called *jesa* are still widely performed on death anniversaries and at the harvest festival Chuseok, many people who perform them identify as Buddhist, Christian or nonreligious. Vietnam's Temple of Literature in Hanoi, founded in 1070 to honor Confucius, is both a monument and a place where students still come before exams.

No one can count Confucians, because there is no membership to count. What can be said is that Confucian ideas about family, education, respect for elders and public service shape hundreds of millions of lives, including many in Chicago's Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities. The lesson for a student of religion is about the lens itself. The category religion was shaped in the West around creeds and churches, and some of the world's great traditions do not fit it neatly. The next chapter meets one of them, Daoism, which the same families often practice at the same time.

words.d: the modern Chinese word for religion, which took on that meaning through Japanese in the late nineteenth century
teaching; the older Chinese category that covered Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism
sanjiao: Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism, long practiced side by side in China
a scholarly label for Confucianism as a human-centered teaching with religious dimensions such as Heaven and ancestral rites
Korean Confucian rites of remembrance for ancestors, held on death anniversaries and at festivals

look.title: The Line on the Form
look.text: A hospital admission form in Chicago has a line marked Religion. A grandmother from Taiwan keeps her parents' tablets on a shelf, sweeps their graves at Qingming, visits a Buddhist temple at New Year and has a Daoist priest for funerals. She reads the Analects to her grandchildren. Her granddaughter, filling out the form, does not know what to write.
look.prompt: What could the granddaughter write, and what would each answer leave out? What does the difficulty tell you about the word religion, and what might the hospital actually need to know?

check.q: Before the nineteenth century, how did Chinese speakers usually classify Confucianism?
choices: As zongjiao, a religion
As a jiao, a teaching, alongside Daoism and Buddhism
As a branch of Buddhism
As a political party
check.why: The word zongjiao took on the meaning religion only later; traditionally Confucianism was one of the three teachings, sanjiao.

It has no priesthood

The list of Five Classics chosen by the Han
The Confucian word for filial piety
The first chapter of the Daodejing
review.why: Zhou texts said Heaven gave the mandate to the virtuous and took it from cruel rulers; it could be lost.

review.q: Which statement about the Analects is accurate?
choices: Confucius wrote it in his last years
It was compiled by his followers over generations from his sayings and dialogues
It is a long treatise on government in ten chapters
It was first written in Latin by Jesuits
review.why: The Lunyu is a collection of sayings assembled by disciples and their students across the fifth to third centuries BCE.

Li replaces ren once a person is educated
Ren is the inner humane heart; li is the outward ritual form through which it acts
Ren belongs to rulers and li to subjects
review.why: Confucius asked what a person without ren has to do with rites; li is the form ren takes in practice.

Mencius
Zengzi
A Legalist such as Han Feizi
review.why: Confucius said father and son shield each other; Legalists put state law above family loyalty.

choices: Whether human nature is good or must be made good by effort
Whether the Analects should be translated
Whether Heaven exists
Whether the Qin dynasty was legitimate
review.why: Mencius taught the four sprouts of inborn goodness; Xunzi taught that goodness is the product of ritual and training.

They selected officials by testing knowledge of the Confucian classics for thirteen centuries
They chose Daoist priests for temples

review.why: From 605 to 1905 CE the examinations on the classics, later the Four Books with Zhu Xi's notes, staffed the government.

Standing firm
Following his heart's desire without overstepping what is right
Having no doubts
